Hi all!

Apologies for the trouble with this

Everything is running for me just fine, and I just re-installed from GitHub just to be sure.  I am attaching the files & script I used.

That error message does suggest that nothing is being read from timeperiods.txt, because normally it would say e.g. "The times in your timeperiods file are: 30 100." or something like that.

My best guess it is something to do with an operating system like Windows mis-reading line-endings, or some such(?)

You can check just the reading/loading of the timeperiods file with:

timeperiods = read_times_fn(inputs=NULL, timesfn="timeperiods.txt")
timeperiods

For me, this returns:

[1]  30 100

...which seems correct.

I'm attaching all of the files I used (just yours, renamed in some cases).

Cheers,
Nick

Hi Nick, thanks for the quick answer.

I checked if the problem is with the returns at the end of lines. Windows use CR+LF, Unix uses only LF. I used Notepad++ to replace CR+LF by LF alone, and tried to re-read, the data, but I still have the same issue:

"Error in section_the_tree(inputs = BioGeoBEARS_run_object_DEC, make_master_table = TRUE,  :
  STOP ERROR in section_the_tree(): the timeperiods file *HAS* to have an oldest time that is older than the bottom node in your tree.  Use the function prt() to get a table of node ages for your tree. The oldest node age in your tree is: 23.170860381. The times in your timeperiods file are: ."

It thus seems that the problem is not with the input file, or at least not with the returns.
Is there any other way of feeding this data to BioGeoBEARS? Perhaps directly from an R object?

Thanks,
Ivan

messages.subject: weird result in clado_events_tables
messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I have a weird thing showing up in my RES_clado_events_tables that I can't readily explain. I fit a time-stratified DEC model on my tree, then performed biogeographic stochastic mapping. I am trying to isolate individual events from the cladogenetic event tables for downstream analyses. My tree has fossils and living species, which might be relevant to the problem.

In this screenshot, I'm showing two rows from the cladogenetic event table from stochastic map #1, corresponding to a single branch on my tree. This branch is a tip (not a fossil), and it's pretty long, stretching across two time-bins (hence the two rows for stratum 1 and 2). I can send the actual files if there is a bigger problem than just my misinterpreting the table.

The species is found in both region A and C, which happens to correspond to range 10 (of 120 possible combinations). I know that the ancestral node (node 2130) was reconstructed in region C (range 4) in this particular stochastic map. The plots of the ancestral reconstruction are consistent with this. What I want to know is the date on this branch the dispersal to A occurred (change from C to AC).

What's weird is that there are no anagenetic events listed here, which I assume would have to happen for a move from C to AC over a branch. The column "sampled_states_AT_nodes" gives two states for each stratum: stratum 1 is reconstructed as AC, while stratum 2 is reconstructed at C. Does this mean that the dispersal event occurred at some point during stratum 2, before stratum 1? Why isn't there an exact value for the event date in the anagenetic event table?

I've been using custom code for parsing stochastic map output for several years now. Is it possible that the structure of the clado_events_tables or anything else has changed recently? Am I simply misinterpreting the table?

Thank you for your help,
Liz

messages.subject: Stratified analyses resulting in unexpected estimates
messages.subject_clean: Stratified analyses resulting in unexpected estimates
messages.body_plain:
Hello everyone

I am relatively new to BioGeoBEARS, but already excited with all the possibilities and flexibility of the package!

I have been able to go through the examples, and also run simple analyses with my own data, and now I am trying to run a stratified analysis. I have been able to load the time periods and run the analysis, but the results are quite unexpected. Only by virtue of loading the time periods and using section_the_tree (and without loading additional distance matrices, etc), the results are quite different from the unconstrained analysis. Not only that, some of the estimates are seemingly wrong: even though the model does not include a J free parameter, some of the estimates are going e.g. from area M to area L without the ancestor going through the ML state as would be expected (compare the nodes highlighted in red in the attached figures spider_stratified and spider_unconstrained).

I thought this could be something specific to my dataset, but I tried to replicate the issue with the Psychotria example data and I have similar results: the estimates are very different in the unconstrained vs. stratified analyses, even though the dispersal probabilities, areas allowed, etc. are exactly the same in both time slices (compare attached Psychotria_DEC_stratified.pdf and Psychotria_DEC_unconstrained.pdf). I also attached the exact same inputs and script of this Psychotria analysis so you can replicate the issue.

My main question is: is this huge effect on the estimates to be expected only by introducing the time slices? And how can the stratified reconstruction give estimates that should NOT be allowed by the model (e.g. a cladogenetic A -> B transition in a model that does not have a J free parameter)?

Many thanks for any clarifications regarding this!
Best regards,
Ivan
--
Dr. Ivan L. F. Magalhaes

Hi -- for this one, I can see that the log-likelihoods and the parameters are different, so you wouldn't expect the ancestral state estimates to be the same.

The fact that the initial DEC model you show has d=0.01, e=0.01 suggests that the optimizer failed to move off of the default starting values, which are typically d=0.01, e=0.01.  This may be an issue with the optimizer, I believe a few months back we found that changing from

$use_optimix = "GenSA" to
$use_optimix = TRUE

...fixed this.

I know there is another request for help on a time-stratified analysis, I haven't been able to get to complex things however as NZ is back on lockdown at the moment & so the toddler is "sharing" the home office. Hopefully soon!

Cheers!
Nick

messages.body_plain:
Hi Ivan,

Thanks very much for persisting with this -- there was indeed a bug, it was in the uppass calculations for time-stratified ancestral states, so it caused no differences in the log-likelihoods or parameter inferences.  Ancestral states estimates are in most cases dominated by the downpass calculations also (the information flows from the tips down in the downpass, but from the reconstructed root states up in the uppass), but I should have seen this earlier -- I had previously specifically checked the case of comparing non-stratified and time-stratified calculations, and they worked: http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-validation#DEC - the bug was exceedingly dumb once I saw it!

To get the bug fix from GitHub:

library(devtools)
devtools::install_github(repo="nmatzke/BioGeoBEARS", INSTALL_opts="--byte-compile")

PS: Pasted below, I have the Psychotria example with non-stratified and time-stratified (with constant 1.0s in the dispersal matrix) models now returning the same ancestral states as each other, and as the validation graphics. Script & input files attached.

Cheers!
Nick
